title: Qualcomm Backs Indian Smart Ring Startup Ultrahuman in $70 Million Bet on Body Computing
excerpt: Bengaluru-based Ultrahuman, valued at $365 million, plans to transform its health-tracking ring into a full computing platform with Qualcomm's silicon.
body:
• Ultrahuman raised $70 million from Qualcomm Ventures, Labcorp, Alpha Wave, and others, valuing the company at $365 million — triple its 2023 valuation.
  • The startup is collaborating with Qualcomm to build a new ring powered by the chipmaker's silicon, enabling on-device software and reducing reliance on smartphones.
  • With $140 million in annual revenue and 800,000 rings sold, Ultrahuman is exploring use cases from gesture control for Meta Glasses to AI interactions.
  • A software update due by end of September will bring game controller and developer platform capabilities to existing rings.

Ultrahuman, the Bengaluru-based startup that has emerged as one of the most formidable challengers to Oura and Samsung in the smart ring market, has raised $70 million in a funding round that signals a pivot from health tracking to something far more ambitious: turning a ring into a computer.

The round values the company at $365 million, roughly three times its $120 million valuation from 2023. Qualcomm Ventures led the investment alongside U.S. diagnostics giant Labcorp, Alpha Wave, Blume Ventures, Nexus Venture Partners, and Alteria Capital. The financing comprises $65 million in primary equity and $5 million in debt, founder and CEO Mohit Kumar told TechCrunch.

From Tracker to Computing Platform

At the heart of the deal is a hardware collaboration with Qualcomm. Ultrahuman is developing a new ring that will run on Qualcomm's silicon alongside its current Nordic Semiconductor chips, adding computing power that allows software and algorithms to run directly on the device rather than routing everything through a phone or the cloud.

"All ring devices today are like trackers. You put on the ring, it measures your heart rate, your movement, your sleep. We want to make the ring more like a computer."

— Mohit Kumar, Founder and CEO, Ultrahuman

The vision extends well beyond health metrics. Kumar said developers could eventually build their own programs for the ring, while Ultrahuman is exploring applications including gesture-based pointing and mouse control, game controllers, car keys, and interfaces for AI interaction. In an interview, chief business officer Bhuvan Srinivasan suggested the ring could work as a gesture controller for devices like Meta's smart glasses — a health tracker by night, an input device by day.

Some of these capabilities will not require waiting for the Qualcomm-powered hardware. Kumar said a software update due by the end of September will bring game controller functionality and a developer platform to the existing Ring Air and Ring Pro models.

A $140 Million Revenue Business

The funding comes as Ultrahuman's core business continues to accelerate. The company is running at a $140 million annual revenue rate, up roughly 45% year-over-year, and expects to hit $200 million by January 2027. It has sold approximately 800,000 rings to date, with about 12% of users subscribing to PowerPlugs, its premium software features.

The U.S. remains Ultrahuman's largest market, contributing about 45% of revenue, though the startup had to temporarily exit the market after a patent dispute with rival Oura. Its redesigned Ring Pro has since returned, and Kumar said demand is running at 18 to 20 times available supply. India accounts for about 11% of revenue.

The startup, co-founded by Kumar and Vatsal Singhal in 2019, originally launched with continuous glucose monitors before pivoting to smart rings. Its ecosystem now includes the Ultrahuman Ring, Blood Vision blood testing, M1 and M2 continuous glucose monitors, Ultrahuman Home environmental sensor, and the Jade AI platform.

Path to IPO

Unlike Oura, which is reportedly eyeing a September IPO, Ultrahuman is charting a more measured public market timeline. Kumar said the company wants to demonstrate eight quarters of profitability before listing, a milestone he expects to reach no earlier than 2028. The company may not be profitable this year due to investments in physical retail locations, brand building, and clinical research.

"The future of AI is personal, ambient, and always on. Ultrahuman is pioneering a new generation of personal AI devices that make personalized insights effortless."

— Quinn Li, Global Head, Qualcomm Ventures

The Labcorp investment also opens a new front in health diagnostics. The two companies are exploring whether blood-flow signals from the ring, combined with blood-test data, could help identify risks in cardiovascular health, fertility, and aging — potentially bridging consumer wearables and clinical diagnostics in ways that neither company has attempted alone.
